title: The Academy Question: Should Gujarat Titans Invest More in Talent Development?
dek: Should Gujarat Titans invest more in developing their own talent? How much of their batting already comes from young players is the place to start.
excerpt: Since 2018, batters aged twenty-three or under have faced a larger share of Gujarat Titans' balls than the league average. That is the baseline any academy investment would aim to change.
author: CricField Editorial Desk
keyTakeaways: Batters aged twenty-three or under faced {{ev:ac-m}} of Gujarat Titans' balls since 2018, against {{ev:ac-o}} for the rest of the IPL.

sections.heading: The Academy Case
body: An academy costs money every year and pays off years later, if at all. The case for one rests on whether young players can win a place, and whether the franchise gives them the chance.
Since 2018, batters aged twenty-three or under have faced {{ev:ac-m}} of Gujarat Titans' balls, against {{ev:ac-o}} for the rest of the IPL.

sections.heading: Who Gets the Chances
body: Gujarat Titans already give young batters more of the strike than most, which suggests an academy pipeline would find a route into the side.
The chart tracks the share season by season.

sections.heading: Proposal: What to Invest In
body: Proposal: an academy focused on the roles the auction supplies worst, such as wrist spin and death bowling, rather than on general development.

sections.heading: Data Limits
body: Birth dates are known for batters facing {{ev:ac-cover}} of Gujarat Titans' balls. Bowling is not included because bowlers' birth-date coverage is thinner still.
Academy spending and graduates are not in the warehouse.

sections.heading: CricField Verdict: Invest Where the Market Fails
body: Gujarat Titans should invest in development where the auction is weakest and where their selection policy will give graduates a real chance.
Measuring the return needs academy records that the franchise holds and this warehouse does not.
